questions.prompt: What is the weighting of this brain scan?
questions.explain: Short TR (500 ms) and short TE (12 ms) give T1 weighting — fat/white matter bright, CSF dark.

questions.prompt: And the weighting of this one?
questions.explain: Long TR (4000 ms) and long TE (100 ms) give T2 weighting — fluid (CSF) is bright.

questions.prompt: Long TR but short TE — what weighting is this?
questions.explain: Long TR removes T1 weighting and short TE removes T2 weighting — what's left is proton-density: signal tracks tissue water content (grey > white, CSF intermediate).

questions.prompt: Which sequence is this — note the dark CSF in the ventricles despite the T2-like brightness elsewhere?
questions.explain: Heavily T2-weighted but with CSF nulled by a long TI (~2500 ms) = FLAIR — the workhorse for periventricular lesions.

questions.prompt: This image shows bright vessels with no contrast injection. What technique produced it?
questions.explain: Time-of-flight (TOF) MRA relies on inflow enhancement — fresh unsaturated blood entering the slice is bright against saturated stationary tissue. No contrast needed.

questions.prompt: A bright focus appears on this diffusion-weighted image of an acute-stroke patient. What does restricted diffusion most likely indicate here?
questions.explain: Restricted diffusion (bright DWI / dark ADC) is the hallmark of an acute infarct — cytotoxic oedema traps water. Always confirm on the ADC map to exclude T2 shine-through.

questions.prompt: Which sequence is best for detecting microhaemorrhages and iron, like the dark foci shown here?
questions.explain: SWI exploits the strong susceptibility of blood products / iron / calcium — they bloom dark. It is the most sensitive sequence for microbleeds and mineralisation.

questions.prompt: A mass enhances brightly on this post-gadolinium T1 scan. Why does gadolinium make it bright?
options: Gadolinium shortens T1 where it leaks through a broken blood-brain barrier
questions.explain: Gadolinium is paramagnetic — it shortens nearby T1, so tissue brightens on T1-weighting. It only reaches the extravascular space where the blood-brain barrier is broken, so enhancement marks BBB breakdown (tumour, active inflammation).

questions.prompt: This is a quantitative perfusion map. A mass shows markedly RAISED values here. Which map is it, and what does that suggest?
options: CBV — high CBV suggests a high-grade tumour
questions.explain: This is the DSC cerebral blood VOLUME map. A tumour grows leaky neovasculature, so raised CBV is a marker of high tumour grade.

questions.prompt: On this DCE permeability map, normal brain is dark but a lesion enhances brightly. What is being measured, and why does normal brain stay dark?
options: Ktrans — the intact blood-brain barrier blocks leakage
CBF — normal brain has no flow
questions.explain: Ktrans is the volume transfer constant (permeability). An intact blood-brain barrier keeps contrast intravascular (Ktrans≈0); tumour/active-lesion vessels leak, so they light up.

questions.prompt: This brain scan shows faint repeating copies of the head across the image. What artifact is this, and along which direction does it propagate?
options: Motion ghosting — along the phase-encode direction
questions.explain: Periodic motion (respiration, pulsation) produces discrete ghosts spaced along the PHASE-ENCODE axis. Averaging (NEX), triggering, or breath-holding reduces them.

questions.prompt: This long-TE gradient-echo image loses signal near the skull base and air interfaces. What causes it, and how do you reduce it?
options: Susceptibility — use spin echo or a shorter TE
questions.explain: Susceptibility differences at air/bone/tissue boundaries dephase spins — worst on long-TE gradient echo. A spin echo's 180° pulse refocuses the dephasing, and a shorter TE gives less time to dephase.

questions.prompt: At this fat–water boundary in the knee there is a dark/bright misregistration band along the readout. What is it, and the fix?
options: Chemical shift — raise the receiver bandwidth (or fat-suppress)
questions.explain: Fat and water resonate ~3.5 ppm apart, so they map to slightly different readout positions — a shift at fat–water borders. A higher receiver bandwidth (or fat suppression) shrinks it.
